overview: The Ashikaga shoguns governed from Kyoto, but shared Japan’s political world with emperors, temples and powerful provincial lords. The indexed span is 1336 to 1573; its surviving map shapes instead run from 1333 to 1492. Neither outline nor label means uniform shogunal control over every community.

periods.title: Rival imperial courts
periods.summary: Ashikaga power developed in Kyoto while a competing imperial court remained at Yoshino. Takauji received the shogun’s title in 1338.

periods.title: Consolidation and connections
periods.summary: After the rival courts reunited, Ashikaga rule and elite patronage flourished, with provincial power still shaping political life.

periods.title: War and shrinking authority
periods.summary: The Onin War devastated Kyoto. Regional lords gained room to act, while Ashikaga prestige outlasted much of their practical control.

items.text: Ashikaga Takauji helped overthrow the Kamakura government, then broke with Emperor Go-Daigo. His new Kyoto administration emerged in 1336. The imperial split and his appointment as shogun in 1338 explain why museums use several starting dates for this complicated transition.

The shogunate was not an all-powerful national command centre. Provincial daimyo influenced both politics and culture. Rivalries helped produce the Onin War of 1467 to 1477, damaging Kyoto and weakening the government that was supposed to coordinate warrior rule.

Yoshimitsu sent an embassy to Ming China in 1401, beginning a new era of licensed official exchange. Japan received copper coins and silk thread, while sulfur, swords and folding fans travelled the other way. Imported money helped sustain Japanese commerce.

Trade licenses used a clever anti-forgery device: writing crossed the edge of a document onto a register. Officials matched the two halves of the characters. It was a paper puzzle with serious consequences for whether a ship could trade.

At sixteenth-century Ichijodani, a typical small house plot had a frontage of about six metres, a well and a backyard toilet. Other houses lacked their own facilities. Even a castle town needed everyday arrangements for water and waste.

Ichijodani bead makers left unfinished crystal prayer beads, pieces broken during drilling and polishing stones. These workshop failures are useful discoveries: a perfect bead shows the result, while a broken one can reveal how the craftsperson tried to make it.

Medicine-compounding tools and a fragment of the Chinese medical text Tangye bencao helped identify a probable doctor’s residence at Ichijodani. The museum also records scholars editing and printing medical books there. Medical learning travelled alongside merchants, monks and refugees from war.

A medical manuscript completed just after this period supplies a further window into earlier practice. Manase Dosan’s Keitekishu, presented to the emperor in 1574, assembled more than thirty years of treatment records. Its surviving autograph shows a physician organising experience into a substantial reference work.

The Hiroshima museum’s reconstruction of fourteenth-century Kusado Sengen separates a craft household’s earthen work floor from its wooden living floor. Its imagined family scenes illustrate archaeological and pictorial evidence; they are not records of one named family caught in a particular moment.

Kusado Sengen’s reconstructed market includes fish, shellfish, seaweed, salt, rice, beans and vegetables. Excavated canals help explain how supplies arrived by boat. It is a useful reminder that the history of warrior government also happened beside food stalls and loading places.

Women could participate in government through writing. At the imperial court, female attendants transmitted a sovereign’s wishes in letters known as nyobo hosho, which became frequent official documents during the Muromachi and Sengoku periods. Household service could involve political responsibility.

Sesshu’s ink landscape of 1495 served a surprisingly practical purpose: his pupil Josui Soen requested it as evidence that he had learned the master’s painting method. On the journey home, Soen collected poems from six Kyoto monks on the same scroll.

The painting’s inscription also records Sesshu’s study in China and his Japanese artistic predecessors. Its loose-looking ink still forms a carefully structured landscape. Artistic education involved travel, personal instruction and deliberate claims about who had taught whom.

At early shoin-style tea gatherings, Ashikaga collections needed specialist curators. They cared for artworks, arranged their display and prepared tea while the host sat with guests. An elegant afternoon depended on knowledgeable work behind the scenes.

Murata Shuko helped turn attention towards modest Japanese ceramics paired with Chinese utensils. Townspeople’s gatherings increasingly featured hosts making tea before their guests. A cup could become a reason to discuss taste, friendship and the pleasure of an imperfect object.

A surviving Seto tea jar from about 1500 is only 8.3 centimetres tall, with thick brown glaze and splashes around its neck and shoulder. Museum treasures can be small enough to fit in a hand; cultural importance does not require castle-sized packaging.

A tiny Japanese sample is “糸ざくら” (ito-zakura), “weeping cherry.” It appears in the museum’s transcription of Ashikaga Yoshiaki’s poem for a 1568 cherry-viewing gathering at Nanyo-ji. This is a transmitted poem in modern transcription, not a newly verified autograph.

Ichijodani belonged to the regional Asakura family. Nobunaga’s army burned the town in 1573, showing how the final years of Ashikaga rule could end violently far from Kyoto too. Its destruction must not be mistaken for the fate of every Japanese town.

Excavations at Ichijodani began in 1967. The museum reports more than 1.7 million recovered items, bringing streets, workshops and household routines back into view. Political chronicles name commanders; archaeology also lets us meet the people who filled containers, repaired tools and fetched water.

ending.text: Oda Nobunaga forced the last Ashikaga shogun, Yoshiaki, out of Kyoto in 1573. The shogunate ended, but regional warfare and Japanese communities continued. Its artistic practices, institutions and memories survived the loss of the ruling government.
